column3: It closely joins sole divinity, praise, judgment, and return to God, directly reinforcing the focus's declaration and closing praise.
It directly commands calling on God with religion made sincere for Him, supplying the focus's central practice.
Its praise of God as Lord of all worlds follows the end of wrongdoing, adding a judgment setting to the focus's praise.
It shows sincere invocation in danger and the later return to association, exposing the fragility that the focus's sincerity excludes.
It repeats sole divinity and names God Lord of the mighty Throne, strengthening the focus's exclusive addressee.
The demonstration of reviving the dead broadly supports divine living power, but adds little to the focus's invocation.
It supplies the exact praise of God as Lord of all worlds, though the formula has already appeared.
It explicitly orders life, death, and renewed life under one divine agency, clarifying the title of the Living.
It directly combines upright worship, calling on God sincerely, and return after creation.
It identifies the sincere servants as exempt from Satan's reach, adding a protective consequence of the focus's sincerity.
It exactly declares God the Living and sole deity, the central identity grounding the focus's call.
Its sign of reviving dead land gives only a broad resurrection analogy, not a direct account of sincere invocation.
It makes sincere religion for God the explicit command and places it within worship, prayer, and almsgiving.
It assigns death and life to God alone, reinforcing the Living God's unique agency after the fuller sequence in 22:66.
It repeats the closing praise formula but adds no new setting beyond earlier instances.
Its call toward one who turns away gives only a distant contrast to calling the one Living God.
It expands the praise of the Lord of all worlds to the Lord of heavens and earth.
It denies ownership to those invoked besides God, directly explaining why the focus's call must exclude rivals.
It places the exact praise of the Lord of all worlds as the culmination of the inhabitants' invocation in the Garden.
It recalls the failure of former objects of invocation besides God, a direct same-surah contrast to the focus.
It names the Living who never dies and couples reliance on Him with praise, closely illuminating the focus's address.
It concerns a prophet's persistent call to his people, not invocation of the sole deity.
It joins sole divinity to God's beautiful names, anticipating the directed manner of calling on Him.
It depicts danger stripping worship to sincere invocation of God and links rescue to gratitude.
It locates the exact praise formula at the conclusion of just eschatological judgment.
The messenger's call to believe in the Lord is related guidance, but not the focus's direct invocation.
It repeats crisis-born sincere invocation and adds the varied responses after rescue, though this is now partly redundant.
The question about reviving decayed bones offers only a limited resurrection backdrop to the Living God.
It explicitly commands calling on God through His beautiful names and rejecting distortion of them.
It directly couples God's giving life and death with the final return to Him.
It repeats the Living, self-sustaining sole God and expands His unceasing governance over creation.
It dedicates worship, life, and death to God, Lord of all worlds, integrating the focus's devotion, life, and praise.
It displays divine control over life emerging from death and challenges turning away, but lacks the invocation command.
Calling for destruction in punishment provides a negative contrast to directed invocation, with little further clarification.
It explicitly moves life from death, death from life, and resurrection from the earth, directly supporting the Living God's power.
Its communal call to good concerns human exhortation rather than sincere calling upon God.
It repeats sole divinity while adding God's knowledge of the unseen and seen, but not the focus's devotional action.
The public repetition of Noah's call adds no distinct understanding after the earlier human-call example.
The divine and angelic testimony to sole divinity adds a public witness to the focus's exclusive confession.
Its question whether idols hear when called directly contrasts them with the Living God addressed in the focus.
It repeats sole divinity and God's lordship over the Throne, though it does not develop invocation.
It again names sincere servants as exceptional, largely repeating the contribution of 15:40.
It repeats sole divinity with mercy, but contributes little beyond the earlier formulations.
The bare pairing of living and dead does not clarify the focus's divine identity or sincere call.
It identifies God alone as deity and unlimited in knowledge, reinforcing exclusive devotion without adding the call.
The summons to a dreadful event is a different kind of call and only loosely relates to the focus.
It declares sole divinity and commands taking God as guardian, supporting exclusive reliance.
Zechariah's personal prayer illustrates that God hears supplication, but does not address exclusive religion.
It forbids calling on another god, repeats sole divinity, and joins judgment and return to God.
It states God's nearness and response to the caller, directly grounding the focus's call to the Living one who answers.
It explicitly commands worshipping God with religion sincerely made His.
It shows called associates failing to respond before punishment, a direct counterexample to the focus's true addressee.
Its sole-divinity formula occurs within embryonic formation and adds little to the focus's invocation.
It plainly states that those invoked besides God neither hear nor answer and will reject the association.
Its argument that multiple gods would corrupt the heavens and earth supports the focus's exclusive deity claim.
It declares that what is called to besides God has no valid call in either world and returns all to God.
It combines praise with God's hearing of prayer, connecting the focus's invocation and praise.
Its claim of being sincere for God is communal and polemical, without developing calling upon Him.
It rejects invented objects of worship and commands worship of God alone as the upright religion.
Its question about being brought out alive offers only a general resurrection connection.
It repeats sole divinity and reliance on God, but is substantially redundant with earlier formulations.
The competing calls toward Fire and toward forgiveness provide a limited contrast to directed divine calling.
It identifies the sole Creator and commands worship of Him, supporting the focus's exclusive devotion.
It affirms God's revival of the dead and recording of deeds, adding an accountability horizon to divine life.
It closely repeats worship of God with religion sincerely made His.
The futile call of disbelievers in the Fire contrasts with the focus's timely, sincere invocation in the same surah.
It commands following revelation from the sole deity and turning from associators, but adds little about invocation.
Its claim of an exclusive hereafter and challenge to wish for death does not clarify the focus.
The failure to answer challengers is used to affirm sole divinity, but only indirectly concerns calling on God.
It portrays leaders who call people to the Fire, sharply contrasting the focus's call to the Living God.
It explicitly commands worshipping God with religion sincerely made His and grounds it in revealed truth.
It depicts disbelievers as unable to hear a call, a contrast that highlights responsive divine hearing.
It exposes religious intermediaries as rival lords and reasserts worship of one God, clarifying what sincere religion excludes.
It joins sole divinity, God's giving life and death, and the command to believe and follow.
It repeats sole divinity and adds the certain gathering for the Day of Resurrection.
Its death-and-revival episode demonstrates divine power, but only broadly relates to the Living God.
Its creation argument ends in sole divinity, yet its formation details do not clarify the focus's call.
Making every living thing from water supplies a broad creation image of life, without the focus's devotional relation.
It seeks that religion belong wholly to God, a related public expression of exclusive religion.
It challenges a rival claim to give life and death, reinforcing that these powers belong uniquely to God.
It attributes creation and command to God, Lord of all worlds, adding universal sovereignty to the focus's praise.
It states that people call on God alone in distress and forget their associates, directly matching exclusive invocation.
It declares pure religion belongs to God and rejects intermediaries claimed to bring people near to Him.
It contrasts the call to salvation with the call to Fire in the same surah, framing the stakes of response.
The isolated title God of humankind adds no material clarification after the fuller sole-divinity declarations.
It depicts a servant calling on God amid a crowd, but adds little about sincerity or divine response.
It forbids calling powerless beings besides God and directs submission to the Lord of all worlds.
The term for what the Garden's people request only faintly relates to invocation and adds no clear link.
Its exclusive worldly adornment for believers in the Hereafter does not clarify the focus's pure religion.
The messenger's call to a straight path is human guidance rather than invocation of God.
The measured descent of things from divine stores does not illuminate the focus's central themes.
It forbids calling on anything besides God that cannot benefit or harm, directly protecting exclusive invocation.
The parable of a good word and rooted tree does not add a specific connection to the focus.
It identifies the one who answers the distressed caller and asks whether any god can be with God.
The pilgrimage regulations being for God do not materially clarify the focus's invocation or divine life.
Its denial that the dead and turning deaf can hear a call contrasts with the Living God who can answer.
Inheritance allocations do not illuminate exclusive invocation, divine life, or praise.
It presents God's call as bringing people out from the earth, extending divine calling to resurrection.
Its near-day warning and absence of an accepted intercessor supply only a broad same-surah judgment backdrop.
It depicts humble, secret calling on God for deliverance and the promised response of gratitude, though earlier crisis scenes cover much of it.
It directly commands calling upon God and promises His response, making it the clearest missing complement to the focus's command of invocation.
It forbids worshipping what is called upon besides God and commands submission to the Lord of all worlds, immediately extending the focus's exclusivity.
It contrasts calling to association with calling to the Mighty Forgiver, supplying the same-surah opposition to the focus's sincere call.
It identifies God as Lord, creator of all things, and sole deity before commanding worship, grounding the focus's address in the same-surah argument.
It declares that the true call belongs to God and that those called besides Him do not answer, directly defining valid invocation.
It shows that distress at sea makes every invoked being vanish except God, a close crisis counterpart to sincere exclusive calling.
It permits calling upon God by His names and ends with praise, linking invocation and the focus's doxology.
It declares no deity except God and commands worship of Him, a foundational formulation of the focus's exclusive devotion.
It gives the recurring prophetic message that there is no deity but God, therefore worship Him.
Jonah's confession of God's sole divinity within distress gives a concrete model of exclusive appeal.
It condemns calling upon another god without proof, directly delimiting the focus's sincere religion.
It explicitly forbids invoking another god alongside God, closely matching the focus's exclusion of rivals.
It challenges people to call alleged partners who possess nothing, directly contrasting false and true invocation.
It joins sole creatorship, provision, and sole divinity, then asks why people turn away from God.
It challenges alleged partners to show any share in creation, exposing the basislessness of calling on them.
It asks who removes harm if God wills it and denies the efficacy of those called besides Him.
It names God creator of all things and guardian over all things, expanding the divine sufficiency assumed by the focus's call.
It rejects worship of others despite knowledge of God, providing a direct contrast to religion made sincere for Him.
It commands worship of God who created the celestial signs rather than worshipping the signs themselves.
It declares God to be both the speaker's Lord and the people's Lord and commands worship of Him alone.
It challenges those called besides God to show what they created, directly testing the legitimacy of rival invocation.
It calls those who invoke beings unable to answer until Resurrection the most astray, directly opposing the focus's responsive Living addressee.
It shows claimed gods failing to help their worshippers, exposing invocation of them as fabricated falsehood.
It forbids setting another deity with God, a concise direct boundary for the focus's exclusive call.
It repeats that God is the sole deity and adds His sovereign, holy, and protective names, enriching the focus's divine address.
It declares that there is no deity except God and directs believers to place trust in Him.
It forbids calling upon anyone alongside God in places of worship, directly specifying exclusive invocation.
It states that the servant calls only upon his Lord and associates no one with Him, nearly restating the focus's devotional relation.
Its declaration of God's absolute oneness gives the most concise doctrinal ground for the focus's no-deity-except-Him formula.
It commands worship of God and association of nothing with Him, directly expressing the exclusivity required by sincere religion.
It forbids worshipping besides God what cannot harm or benefit, directly explaining why rival invocation is void.
It asks whether people would call anyone besides God when overwhelming distress comes, a direct test of exclusive appeal.
It states that worship of those called besides God is forbidden, providing a precise boundary for the focus's invocation.
It challenges those who call beings besides God to call them if they are true, directly exposing their impotence.
It states that those called besides God cannot help their callers or themselves.
It asks who provides, hears, sees, and brings forth living from dead, grounding exclusive devotion in God's life-giving governance.
It identifies God as the true Lord and asks what remains after truth except error, supporting the focus's exclusive orientation.
It describes those called besides God as unable to create and as dead rather than living, the sharpest contrast to the Living one.
It forbids taking two gods and declares that God is one, directly reinforcing the no-deity-except-Him formula.
It forbids setting another god beside God, directly protecting the focus's exclusive worship.
It challenges people to call those they claim besides God, who cannot remove or transfer harm.
It closes with praise of God and denies Him any partner in dominion, strongly resonating with the focus's praise and exclusivity.
It requires worship of the one Lord without associating anyone in that worship.
It portrays calling on what can neither harm nor benefit besides God as manifest misguidance.
It identifies God as the Truth and those called besides Him as falsehood, grounding exclusive invocation in that contrast.
It challenges all called beings besides God as unable even to create a fly, directly refuting their claimed efficacy.
It denies God any partner in dominion and affirms His creation and measure of all things.
It describes those taken besides God as unable to create, harm, benefit, cause death, give life, or raise, directly contrasting the Living God.
It rebukes worship of what neither benefits nor harms besides God.
It repeatedly asks whether any god is with God after acts of creation and provision, strengthening the focus's exclusive deity claim.
It couples creation, provision, and resurrection with the question whether any god is with God.
It asks where the claimed partners are on the Day of Judgment, exposing the final absence of rival addressees.
It repeats the summons to produce claimed partners before God, reinforcing the judgment of association.
It shows people calling their Lord sincerely when hardship touches them, then reverting after mercy, closely paralleling the crisis-invocation pattern.
It attributes creation, provision, death, and life to God and asks whether any associates can do any of this.
It records the confession that God created the heavens and earth, then questions why people are turned away.
It states that people take gods besides God hoping for help, a direct contrast to calling the only effective helper.
It records the rejection of the declaration that there is no deity except God, supplying the polemical opposite of the focus's confession.
Abraham's disavowal of what his people worship establishes a direct ancestral model of exclusive devotion.
It attributes life and death to God and gathers all for the Day of Resurrection.
It asks whether they have any god other than God, affirming His transcendence above association.
It assigns dominion, life, death, and power over all things to God.
